analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery stores from price gouging and from setting prices based on surveillance of individual shoppers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2026 with 11 Senate cosponsors and sent to the Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for grocery stores to charge 'grossly excessive' prices, with a cost-based defense so stores can still pass along legitimate cost increases. It would also ban stores from setting a shopper's individual price using surveillance data — including facial recognition — and would prohibit large stores from using electronic shelf labels, the digital price tags that can be changed remotely. Enforcement would fall to the FTC, state attorneys general, and private consumers, who could sue for damages of at least $3,000 per violation, tripled for knowing violations. The bill has been referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and has not moved since introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Grocery shoppers, especially lower-income households spending a large share of income on food, gain protection from extreme price spikes and from stores charging individual shoppers more based on data collected about them. The bill's enforcement tools — lawsuits with attorney's fees, tripled damages for willful violations, and unenforceable pre-dispute arbitration clauses — are designed to be usable by ordinary consumers, not just regulators.

how_it_helps.text: It bans retail food stores from selling items at 'grossly excessive' prices, with an exception only when the increase comes from the store's own uncontrollable costs, and lets the FTC set a benchmark — it suggests considering prices 120% or more above the prior six-month market average.

It prohibits stores from setting an individual's price based on personal information gathered through surveillance technology, including facial recognition, and bans the technology-driven version of the practice: electronic shelf labels that could change a displayed price for a specific shopper.
It requires large stores to post plain-language signage if they use facial recognition, and generally bans digital price tags in stores over 10,000 square feet.

It gives shoppers the right to sue: actual damages or $3,000 per violation, tripled for willful violations, with attorney's fees, and it makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims. State attorneys general can also sue.

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery retailers would bear compliance costs, enforcement exposure, and new lawsuit risk; makers of electronic shelf labels and facial recognition systems would lose a sales channel. Some compliance costs could be passed to shoppers as marginally higher baseline prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large grocery chains and retail-tech vendors

drawbacks.text: The 'grossly excessive price' standard is vague: the FTC would decide what counts as a market and how high a price must be before it is illegal, and critics of such caps argue this can deter stores from raising prices even when their own costs rise, potentially causing shortages.

The flat ban on electronic shelf labels applies to any store over 10,000 square feet, even where the labels are used only to show sale prices or update tags faster, a restriction retailers say adds labor costs that can be passed on to shoppers.

The bill's private right of action, with $3,000 statutory damages per violation and attorney's fees, could generate litigation against stores over pricing practices that turn out to be lawful cost pass-throughs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would give consumers real protections against hidden price manipulation and give price-gouging victims a practical way to sue, with fees paid by winning plaintiffs' lawyers and triple damages for knowing violations. The costs are real but limited: enforcement could add compliance friction for stores, the flat electronic-shelf-label ban may delay modest price-tag innovations that have nothing to do with individualized pricing, and the vague 'grossly excessive price' standard puts significant discretionary power in regulators' hands, which could occasionally chill legitimate pricing. On balance, the consumer protections appear to outweigh these drawbacks, though the drafting is loose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 12, 2026, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
No further action — no hearings, markup, floor vote, or House companion action — appears in the action history.
It drew 11 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, in a Senate where 55 Republicans hold a majority, leaving it far short of the support needed to reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's situation has changed; large grocery retailers avoid any new restrictions because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; large grocers avoid new rules

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents; no Senate Republicans support the bill, and it sits in committee in a chamber where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats.

industries.note: The bill caps their ability to raise prices beyond cost increases, bans individualized surveillance-based pricing, outlaws facial recognition in stores without signage, and forces stores over 10,000 square feet back to paper price tags. It also exposes them to $3,000-per-violation lawsuits with fee-shifting.

industries.industry: Electronic shelf label and retail-tech vendors
industries.note: The bill bans the use of electronic shelf labels and digital price displays in large grocery stores, cutting off a growing sales channel.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and in-store surveillance firms
industries.note: Retail use of facial recognition would require conspicuous disclosure, and using biometric data for pricing would be barred except with detailed written consumer consent and no third-party sharing.

industries.industry: Consumer plaintiffs' bar and state attorney general offices
industries.note: The bill creates a private right of action with statutory damages, attorney's fees, and state parens patriae enforcement, funded by a $5 million appropriation for FTC implementation.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in committee with no Republican support in a Senate controlled by Republicans 55-47; unless the Commerce Committee takes it up, it will likely die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
